steps.body: To land **a/b**, take a jumps of size 1/b: 3/4 is three jumps of a four-cut trip. It's chapter 1's stacking, walked out loud — 1/4, 2/4, 3/4 — the top number is simply your **jump count**.

widget.prompt: The 0→1 trip has 4 equal jumps. Slide the marker to 3/4 — count your jumps as you go.
widget.lowFeedback: Keep counting up — 1/4, 2/4… you're not at three jumps yet.
widget.highFeedback: That's the whole trip (4/4 = 1)! Step back one jump.
widget.successFeedback: Three jumps of the four: you're on 3/4, one jump shy of the finish.

predict.prompt: You'll slide to 3/4. Is that before the halfway point, exactly halfway, or past halfway?
predict.reveal: Halfway is 2/4 — two jumps. Three jumps carries you a whole jump beyond the middle of the trip.

cml.actionGoal: Manipulate the model and track how it represents nl fraction.
invariants: The manipulated model and the mathematical relationship for nl fraction must stay consistent.
misconceptions: Changing a visible feature without preserving the relationship that defines nl fraction.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: What change would make the model stop representing the same mathematical relationship?

explanationVariants: The top of 5/6 is the jump count: five jumps of the six-cut trip.
Count the landings: 1/6, 2/6, 3/6, 4/6, 5/6 — you said five names, you took five jumps.

widget.prompt: On a 0→1 line with 6 equal jumps, how many jumps take you to 5/6?

commonErrors.feedback: 6 jumps finish the whole trip — that's 6/6 = 1. 5/6 stops one jump short.
1 jump lands 1/6, the first mark. The TOP number counts the jumps, and it says five.

widget.fallbackFeedback: The top number of 5/6 is your jump count.

steps.body: Count up the line out loud: **1/4, 2/4, 3/4, 4/4** — and 4/4 lands exactly on 1, all the pieces walked. Every landing between 0 and 1 gets a fraction name, and the count-up IS the sequence of names.

explanationVariants: Three jumps of a fourth each: you're standing on 3/4.
Say the landings as you go — 1/4, 2/4, 3/4 — the third name is where the third jump ends.

widget.prompt: Counting by fourths from 0, where do you stand after your THIRD jump?

options.feedback: Third jump, third landing: 3/4 of the way along.
1/3 belongs to a THREE-cut trip. This trip is cut into fourths — three of them is 3/4.

options.label: The number 3
options.feedback: You're still inside the 0→1 trip — landings here are fractions. Three fourth-jumps reach 3/4, not 3.
4/3 flips the jobs — that would be four jumps of a THIRDS trip, past 1! Three fourth-jumps land at 3/4.

steps.body: Line them up along the trail.

widget.prompt: Order these landings from CLOSEST to 0 up to closest to 1.

misorderFeedback.feedback: 4/5 is FOUR jumps out — 2/5 stops at two. Same jump size, so more jumps means farther along.
5/5 is the finish line itself (that's 1) — nothing on this list stands past it.

widget.missFeedback: All four use fifth-size jumps — so the jump COUNT (the top) decides the order.
widget.successFeedback: 1/5, 2/5, 4/5, 5/5 — same jumps, rising counts, and 5/5 caps the trip at 1.

explanationVariants: Two of four jumps is half the trip — 2/4 lands on the very same spot as 1/2.
Half the jumps of the trip cover half its distance: 2/4 and 1/2 are two names for one point.

options.label: Exactly halfway — the same spot as 1/2
options.feedback: Two of four jumps = half the trip. One spot, two names — hold that thought for the next chapter.

options.label: A quarter of the way
options.feedback: A quarter is ONE jump — 1/4. You took two, landing at the halfway point.

options.label: At the number 2
options.feedback: Two fourth-jumps stay well inside the 0→1 trip — they reach the middle, not the number 2.

options.label: Almost at 1
options.feedback: Almost-there is 3/4, three jumps out. Two of four is dead center.

hints: Stops stand at 1/6, 2/6, 3/6… — one per sixth walked.
Kai is standing exactly on his 5th stop.
One stop passed = one sixth walked.
explanationVariants: Five stops means five sixth-jumps walked — Kai stands at 5/6 of the mile, so 5 sixths are behind him.
Match stops to landings: stop 1 is 1/6, stop 2 is 2/6… stop 5 is 5/6. The stop number IS the sixths walked.

widget.prompt: A 1-mile trail has a water stop at every SIXTH of a mile. Kai has reached 5 stops — the fifth is right under his boots. How many sixths of the mile has he walked?

commonErrors.feedback: 1 sixth is what's LEFT ahead of him. The question asks what's behind: five stops, five sixths walked.
6 sixths is the whole mile — but Kai hasn't reached the end. His fifth stop marks 5/6.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Each stop marks one more sixth: the stop number equals the sixths walked.

takeaways: a/b = a jumps of size 1/b — the top is your jump count.
Counting up the line says the names: 1/4, 2/4, 3/4, 4/4 = 1.
Same jump size? The jump count alone sets who's farther along.
steps.teaser: but what if you keep jumping past 1? The line doesn't stop — and neither do fractions.

concept.body: Quick rewind. Walk it on your fingers: for 2/3, count **"one third, two thirds"** — and stop. The top number tells you when to stop counting; the landing under your last finger is the fraction.

explanationVariants: Two jumps of a three-cut trip land on 2/3.
Count: one third, two thirds — stop. That spot is 2/3.

widget.prompt: On a 3-jump line from 0 to 1, where are you after 2 jumps?

options.feedback: Two of the three jumps — 2/3 of the way.
Flipped! 3/2 would be three jumps of a HALVES trip — past 1. Two jumps of thirds is 2/3.

options.label: The number 2
options.feedback: Two third-jumps stay inside the trip — you're at 2/3, not out at 2.
